  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Vignette:
The canister had looked standard, bolted shut and marked with yellow hazard tape, but the pressure gauge had dropped without warning. Elijah Vance was thirty-eight when he cracked the seal on that abandoned munition in a Georgia warehouse. The air shifted instantly, turning sharp and metallic, and within seconds his lungs burned while a heavy vapor clung to his coveralls. He remembered the crackle of his radio, the frantic shouts of his team, and the sudden sting of antiseptic wipes as the medics dragged him toward the decontamination shower. The exposure left his hands trembling for months, but it was the silence that followed that grew heavy. He had come to believe that danger never announced itself; it simply arrived, invisible and fast. In the years that followed, Elijah’s routine slowly hardened. Before stepping into any room, his eyes would trace the doors and windows, counting exits until his shoulders dropped. He was certain that stopping his vigilance would leave him completely exposed. Loud work boots, a dropped toolbox, or a fire alarm could make his breath catch and his muscles lock. He avoided hospitals and ambulances entirely, steering his truck around emergency clinics and turning down the routine physicals his wife, Naomi, gently suggested. What frightened him most was the sudden vulnerability of a quiet room, so he began staying late at the depot, running diagnostics on ordnance that didn’t require it. The clatter of his tools and the steady rhythm of heavy lifting filled his hours. He lingered in break rooms, took extra calls, and volunteered for night watches just to keep the solitude at a distance. At sixty-two, Elijah still carried the weight of that shift change. His current post at the municipal explosives ordinance unit kept him close to the very environment that had betrayed him, which only sharpened the edges of his nerves. When a foreman dropped a steel casing on the concrete floor, the sound still sent him spinning toward the bulkhead, heart hammering against his ribs. The sharp tang of industrial degreaser sometimes drifted from the ventilation shafts, and he would immediately unclip his gear, stepping outside to clear his head. Naomi knew not to touch his back while he was sorting through paperwork; a sudden hand on his shoulder still made him flinch, his breath hitching before he forced himself to turn. He read every space as a map of threats, his eyes constantly tracking air vents, stairwells, and the distance to the nearest exit. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single panic attack, but a quiet erosion. He noticed he could no longer sleep through the night without checking the deadbolt three times, and he saw the distance growing between him and Naomi as he declined dinners, skipped family gatherings, and retreated into the depot’s fluorescent hum. He was most afraid that his own hyperawareness was slowly wiring him into a cage, but he was hoping for a way to stand in a room without counting the doors. He wanted to learn how to let his guard down long enough to hear his wife’s voice without his body bracing for a command, and to work without needing the constant clatter to keep the silence at bay.
